newsitem.title: USA: House defeats tobacco measures, pact criticized.
newsitem.headline: House defeats tobacco measures, pact criticized.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives on Thursday defeated two anti-tobacco measures as public health groups stepped up criticism of aspects of the proposed tobacco litigation settlement.
The Senate defeated two similar measures Wednesday.

One House proposal would have eliminated subsidised crop insurance for tobacco farmers and the other would have taken $14 million out of the crop insurance programme and given it to the Food and Drug Administration to enforce its new rules against teen smoking.

"It is in the interest of America's children," said Representative Marty Meehan, D-Mass., who wanted to give the FDA the full $34 million requested to pay for the new programme requiring ID checks to prevent tobacco sales to underage smokers.

Neither the FDA funding nor the crop plan are directly related to the proposed $368 billion settlement between the tobacco industry and 40 states suing it, which is undergoing White House review. Congress would have to pass legislation to enact that settlement.

Congress is also still wrestling with a proposal, backed by the Senate and President Bill Clinton but not the House, to raise cigarette taxes and use part of the money to expand children's health care coverage.
Meanwhile, the American Cancer Society, the American Lung Association and some lawmakers Thursday separately criticised what they regard as flaws in the proposed tobacco settlement.

Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala and Clinton's domestic policy adviser, Bruce Reed, who are heading the White House task force, met with congressional Democrats to solicit their views.

"There are a lot of flaws in the agreement, and they (the administration) are identifying the flaws," Representative Henry Waxman, a California Democrat who is one of the staunchest foes of tobacco in Congress, said after the meeting.

Shalala said lawmakers cited several concerns, including the disclosure of confidential cigarette industry documents, the breadth of the FDA's power to regulate nicotine and other tobacco ingredients,, enforcement of the agreement, tax deductibility of the payout by the industry, and how it would affect tobacco farmers.
The American Cancer Society and the American Lung Association issued separate critiques of aspects of the settlement proposal.

The cancer society outlined seven areas where the agreement should be made tougher. It also demanded that the industry reveal all confidential documents relevant to public health, and called for a $2-per-pack tax on cigarettes.
"The American Cancer Society supports the right settlement -- but this is not that settlement," said the society's chairman, George Dessart.

The lung association analysed the portions of the settlement that would restrict certain advertising practices by the industry and concluded they would be "a mere inconvenience," and not a real obstacle to peddling a dangerous product.

The association called for stricter terms, including ensuring that ads appear only in publications with an adult audience. Ads should be black and white and have no props or scenery of any type, except the cigarette package -- and the warning label.
